title: Hearing bebop and Dizzy Gillespie
summary: In the mid-1950s she listened to Dizzy at the Royal Roost and wasn't impressed at first, but accepts it created a new sound.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Well, way back, I would say around 1956, before I eventually retired, I was appearing at the Village Vanguard down in the Village; and a friend of mine came and said, 'I want to take you uptown to hear the new music.'
And it was -- Dizzy was at the Royal Roost, I believed it was, with his bop. And I

hadn't paid much attention to the modern bop, or whatever it was at the time.
And so I listened. I wasn't too impressed at the time. First of all, I guess I felt like Louie did when he said, 'If you have to explain it, it's not jazz.'
I think he also called it "Chinese music."

Well, it was pretty hard to take in the beginning, but I guess we can get used to it. I, personally, am not sold on bop. But you can't deny the virtuosity of the instrumentalists who are responsible for it.

And it did create a new sound and gave something to the new young musicians to shoot at. However, I would hope that they would get involved in the fundamentals first instead of starting off on the top.
But that's just a personal opinion.
